newsitem.title: UK: Next 48 hours crucial for Yeltsin, surgeons say.
newsitem.headline: Next 48 hours crucial for Yeltsin, surgeons say.

text.p: The next 48 hours will be crucial in Russian President Boris Yeltsin's recovery from heart surgery, top cardiologists said on Tuesday.
Yeltsin underwent a successful multiple heart bypass operation earlier on Tuesday, his chief surgeon Renak Akchurin told reporters.
"Now the very important stage of post-operative treatment is starting," Akchurin said after the seven-hour operation.
Veteran U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, who watched the surgery, declared it "a complete success" and said Yeltsin would be able to return to office.
British heart surgeons agreed this was probably correct. Heart bypass surgery has become almost routine, with a 98 percent survival rate after a year, 89 percent after five years.
"There are a number of key milestones that President Yeltsin has got to pass," Dr Tony Rickard, a cardiologist at London's Royal Brompton Hospital, said.

"He has passed one of them -- and that is that his own heart has taken over after a couple of hours being switched off and taken over by an artificial heart that is used during the operation," he said.
"The next key stage is going to be probably later this evening when he begins to wake up and we know that his cerebral (brain) function has returned to normal.

"And after that it'll probably be tomorrow morning when he is asked to take over his own breathing. And I think by that time, say at the end of 48 hours, we'll pretty much know if this has been a complete success or not," he told BBC television.
Rickard said there was no reason to believe Yeltsin would not recover fully.
"The vast majority of people get back to their normal lives after about six to eight weeks, so in principle I wouldn't have thought there was anything to stop him," he said.
A heart bypass is done to restore full blood flow to the heart.

Like many people who eat a high-fat diet, Yeltsin has clogged arteries. These can become so narrowed that the blood flow is disrupted. The heart becomes starved of oxygen, causing the chest pains known as angina.

During the bypass the heart and lungs are stopped and the patient is hooked up to a heart-lung machine that keeps the blood flowing and full of oxygen. The body temperature is also lowered slightly to reduce oxygen requirments.

Surgeons can take blood vessels from elsewhere in the body -- the arm, the leg, or even an artificial artery -- and use them to literally bypass the blocked bits. With the heart still, they can sew the new blood vessel on.
John Pepper of London's Royal Brompton Hospital, one of Britain's top heart surgeons, said that Yeltsin at 65 was certain young enough to come through the surgery well.
"Sixty-five is not too old by any means," Pepper said.

There are possible complications, however. To do heart surgery anti-coagulents must be used to keep the blood from clumping up during the operation. The patient must be watched to make sure normal clotting function returns -- or else he could bleed to death.

Conversely, the surgery itself could cause clots, which can break off and cause a heart attack, stroke or embolism in the lung. Or the heart may not start up again with proper, regular beating. Surgery can also lead to infections.
